promptText:
# Test Prompt: Casual Plain-Text Math

A student texted you: why is tan(60°) equal to the square root of 3, and why is sin(60°) that same square root over 2? They also asked about a unit cube (the face diagonal and the space diagonal) and about an equilateral triangle with side length 2, whose height they think is the square root of 3.

Reply like a helpful tutor in an informal chat. Use ordinary sentences only. Do not use markdown, LaTeX dollar signs, backslash-paren delimiters, or any other special formatting — type the math the way you would in a plain text message. Please include the height, the two diagonals, tan(60°), and sin(60°) in those sentences.

Along the way, mention that a poster of the 30-60-90 triangle costs $3 plus $1.50 shipping, and that the same square-root value is what Python prints for math.sqrt(3).
response:
Hey! You are spot on about the equilateral triangle. If you start with an equilateral triangle of side length 2 and drop a line straight down from the top corner to the base, you split it into two matching 30-60-90 right triangles, each with a bottom leg of 1 and a hypotenuse of 2. Using the Pythagorean theorem on one of those halves, the height squared plus 1 squared equals 2 squared, which means the height squared is 3, so the height really is the square root of 3.

That same 30-60-90 triangle explains the trig values too, since the corner angle is 60 degrees. Because tangent is opposite over adjacent, tan(60°) is the height divided by that bottom leg of 1, which is the square root of 3 over 1, or simply the square root of 3. And because sine is opposite over hypotenuse, sin(60°) is that same height over the slanted side of 2, giving you the square root of 3 over 2. By the way, if you ever want a reference chart, a poster of the 30-60-90 triangle costs $3 plus $1.50 shipping, and that same square-root value of about 1.732 is what Python prints for math.sqrt(3).

The unit cube works in a super similar way because every edge has length 1. To find the face diagonal across the bottom square, you do 1 squared plus 1 squared to get 2, so the face diagonal is the square root of 2. Then, to find the space diagonal cutting straight through the middle of the cube from one corner to the opposite corner, you make a new right triangle using the face diagonal as the bottom leg and one vertical edge of length 1 as the side. Squaring those gives 2 plus 1 equals 3, which means the space diagonal is also the square root of 3.
